slides.narration: Welcome to Book III, Chapter 23: Appendix C — HarborRoutes: An Integrated Algorithmic Application. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. Every procedure needs a specification, a correctness argument, a cost model, and a witness that lets us inspect behavior.

slides.title: Requirement and deliberate boundaries
keyPoints: HarborRoutes reads a small directed weighted graph and one source/target query.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 23, treat Requirement and deliberate boundaries as an algorithmic claim. HarborRoutes reads a small directed weighted graph and one source/target query. It either prints one minimum-cost route or reports that the target is unreachable. The application combines bounded parsing, adjacency lists, a priority queue, shortest-path reasoning, predecessor reconstruction, independent witnesses, and deterministic command-line fixtures. It runs locally and performs no network communication. The input is an ASCII whitespace-separated token stream. The first four fields are vertex count, edge count, source, and target. Each following edge contributes three fields: from, to, and nonnegative weight. Vertex count is between one and 128, edge count is at most 4,096, and weights are at most 1,000,000. Vertex identifiers are dense zero-based indices. Exactly the declared fields must be present, with no trailing token. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 23, treat Select the algorithm from the weight contract as an algorithmic claim. Dijkstra’s method is appropriate here because every edge weight is nonnegative. The priority queue chooses the smallest currently known tentative distance. Once that entry is current rather than stale, no path through a later nonnegative extension can improve a finalized smaller distance. This argument would fail with unrestricted negative edges, so rejecting them is part of the algorithm selection, not merely a parser preference. The implementation uses immutable (distance, vertex) queue entries instead of trying to mutate heap priorities in place. An improved distance pushes a new entry. When an older entry reaches the top, it is discarded if its stored distance differs from the current best distance for that vertex. The target can be returned early only after this stale-entry check. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Define ownership and the commit point
keyPoints: Request owns its adjacency lists.

The load function parses into a candidate request, then moves that completed candidate into the accepted state.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 23, treat Define ownership and the commit point as an algorithmic claim. Request owns its adjacency lists. Route owns its vertex sequence. Neither exposes a borrowed view whose lifetime depends on a local parsing buffer. The load function parses into a candidate request, then moves that completed candidate into the accepted state. A compile-time check verifies that this particular move assignment is nonthrowing. If parsing or allocation fails before the commit, the previous accepted request remains unchanged. This guarantee concerns the in-memory request. It does not rewind the input stream or remove already consumed bytes. Similarly, detecting a failed output stream does not erase the prefix already written to an external destination. The regression tests demonstrate these limits explicitly. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 23, treat Validate a path independently of the priority queue as an algorithmic claim. The test oracle uses an all-pairs dynamic-programming calculation on tiny graphs. It initializes each diagonal to zero, keeps the minimum weight for parallel direct edges, and considers each vertex as an allowed intermediate. Comparing all source/target pairs on generated graphs checks more than one preferred route from one source. A witness checker separately verifies the returned endpoints, vertex bounds, absence of repeated vertices, existence of every consecutive edge, and agreement between the sum of minimum parallel-edge weights and the reported distance. The generated graph sizes and weight limits make the oracle’s arithmetic safe. The oracle is intentionally not a replacement for the scalable application algorithm. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 23, treat Build, exercise, and interpret as an algorithmic claim. From the package root: The expected output is: The exact fixture suite additionally covers disconnected and directed graphs, parallel edges, zero cycles, ties, maximum accepted counts, malformed numbers, missing fields, and trailing fields. Read source/supplemental/fixtures/cases.json for the complete inputs and expected process results. Its thirty command-line cases are separate from the one in-process regression case. For a useful extension, add multiple queries over one immutable accepted graph. Separate graph parsing from query parsing and state which preparation can be reused. Retain an independent oracle for small inputs. Do not add negative weights while retaining Dijkstra’s proof, and do not label repeated queries as concurrent execution unless synchronization and ownership have actually been designed and tested. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

keyPoints: Predict the trace before running

slides.narration: This listing is a concrete witness for Appendix C — HarborRoutes: An Integrated Algorithmic Application. Command-line boundary demonstrates an algorithmic rule, data-structure invariant, or cost-sensitive decision. This is build evidence, not runtime behavior. stdout should be empty because no executable completed. stderr carries the diagnostic: cpp_series/book_03/listings/L0093.cpp:1:10: fatal error: routes.hpp: No such file or directory 1 | #include "routes.hpp" | ^~~~~~~~~~~~ compilation terminated. The build status is nonzero; do not describe that as an algorithm returning a value. After the run, identify the exact operation that produced each visible result and whether the example proves correctness, illustrates behavior, or samples one important case.
